snippet.title: This is How One Wrong Decision Destroyed India’s Biggest Airline
snippet.description:
This is How One Wrong Decision Destroyed India’s Biggest Airline ! Aman Sharma
In 1993, Naresh Goyal launched Jet Airways with just four leased aircraft. Thanks to its premium service, the airline quickly became a favorite among travelers and by 2005 had become India's largest domestic airline, generating over $1 billion in revenue.

But success brought overconfidence.

In 2007, Jet Airways acquired the struggling Air Sahara for ₹1,450 crore. What looked like a smart expansion soon turned into a financial nightmare. As debt increased, low-cost rivals like IndiGo, SpiceJet, and GoAir entered the market and changed the aviation industry forever.

Despite its premium reputation, Jet Airways was forced to cut prices while fuel costs and taxes continued to rise. The result was more than ₹8,000 crore in debt.

On 17 April 2019, Jet Airways finally shut down all operations.

But the tragedy didn't end there. In 2023, Naresh Goyal was arrested in a ₹540 crore bank fraud case. During the same period, he lost his wife Anita Goyal to cancer while battling cancer himself.

This is the incredible and heartbreaking story of how India's biggest airline rose to the top—and then came crashing down.

snippet.title: What Iran’s top security official said about June 2025 U.S. and Israeli strikes
snippet.description:
Ali Larijani was secretary of the Supreme National Security Council in charge of Iran’s nuclear negotiations at the time that this 2025 interview was conducted. Iran confirmed he was killed in an Israeli airstrike in March 2026.

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In a wide-ranging conversation in Tehran, Larijani said Iran had pursued every option to resolve the conflict with the U.S. in a peaceful way and warned President Donald Trump against new attacks, saying there was no chance Iran would surrender. It was Larijani’s first interview with foreign media after he was appointed to his role by the late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei following the 12-day war with the U.S. and Israel in June 2025.

Larijani was once a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful Iranian paramilitary force, and served as parliament speaker from 2008 to 2020. In the months preceding the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran in February 2026, Larijani was reportedly in charge of the deadly crackdown on Iranian protesters and tasked with shoring up the Islamic Republic’s existence in case of war.

Larijani spoke through an interpreter with FRONTLINE’s Sebastian Walker on Sept. 22, 2025, for our 2025 documentary, "Strike on Iran: The Nuclear Question." This was Larijani's last on-camera interview with an American news outlet before he was killed. See a more complete description of our process here: https://to.pbs.org/4lVZKzA

snippet.title: Police Bombed MOVE Organizers’ Home in 1985 (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
snippet.description:
An investigation into the 1985 police bombing of the Black revolutionary group MOVE’s headquarters in a middle-class neighborhood in West Philadelphia. (Aired 1987)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

On May 13, 1985, a years-long feud between the Black revolutionary group MOVE and Philadelphia officials reached a bloody culmination that saw police dropping a military-grade bomb in a Black residential neighborhood and allowing the resulting fire to rage. Eleven people were killed at MOVE’s headquarters, five of them children, and 61 neighboring homes were destroyed.

How it happened, and who was responsible, is the focus of the 1987 FRONTLINE documentary, “The Bombing of West Philly.” 

“We have to remember that this nation fought wars to prevent bombs from being dropped on its people in this country,” Novella Williams, a community activist, said in the documentary. “And we sit by and allow a little city government to borrow a helicopter and concoct a bomb with high military explosives, C-4, and drop it on our people? What kind of people are we?” The documentary is a powerful and nuanced exploration of that question, tracing back to the 1970s, when MOVE arose against the backdrop of stark police brutality against Black Philadelphians.

The 1985 bombing and the resulting fire destroyed not just the MOVE compound, but also the homes of frustrated neighbors who had complained about MOVE’s tactics to city officials and begged for their help.

The Philadelphia City Council issued a formal apology for the MOVE bombing in 2020, acknowledging “the fundamental injustice, cruelty, brutality, and inhumanity” of the event. No city officials were ever criminally charged. 

“The Bombing of West Philly” was written, produced and directed by Martin Smith. The correspondent was Leon Dash. The associate producer was Sue Williams. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

The name Ray-Ban literally means “Ban the Rays” — because these glasses were designed to block harsh sun rays and give pilots crystal-clear vision during flight.

By the 1940s, America’s military influence on fashion skyrocketed, and by the 1950s, Hollywood legends made Ray-Ban a global fashion icon.
From military gear to a style statement, Ray-Ban became timeless!

snippet.title: How This One Machine Controls the Future of Technology !
snippet.description:
How This One Machine Controls the Future of Technology ! Aman Sharma
From smartphones and AI chips to fighter jets, modern technology runs on semiconductor chips.

But manufacturing these chips is so difficult that even giants like Apple, Samsung, and Nvidia don't produce the most advanced chips entirely on their own.

The reason? A mind-blowing machine called the EUV Lithography Machine, built exclusively by ASML.

Worth around ₹3,700 crore per unit, it's considered one of the most complex machines ever created. It uses lasers, molten tin, and extreme ultraviolet light to print circuits thousands of times smaller than a human hair.

The technology is so strategic that the United States strictly controls which countries can access it, and China has spent years trying to build its own version without success.

Now, through a major partnership between Tata Electronics and ASML, India is preparing to enter advanced chip manufacturing for the first time.

Could this be the beginning of India's semiconductor revolution?

snippet.title: The 12-Year-Old Bhujia Seller
snippet.description:
A 12-year-old Rajasthani Marwari boy built India’s biggest snack company, beating billion-dollar multinational giants.

In 1919, 12-year-old Haldiram began selling Bhujia for just 2 paise at his grandfather’s shop in Bikaner.

But while all Bhujia sellers used to make it from Besan, he decided to do something crazy that had never been done before.

Since Rajasthanis already liked Moth Dal, he started mixing that with besan to make his Bhujia.

And something amazing happened.

His bhujia became became thinner and crispier, becoming an instant hit in the entire city of Bikaner.

But then, an unexpected tragedy happened - disputes led to a family split in which Haldiram was kicked out of his own business.

That was when a childhood friend gave him 100 rupees, and Haldiram started his business from scratch by selling her wife’s amazing Moong Dal.

What happened next was unbelievable.

Haldiram started selling Indian namkeens in modern packaging across India.

But since Indians already loved local namkeens, Halidram’s did it while spending almost nothing on marketing.

Today, Haldiram’s sells 400+ packaged products across 80+ countries, earning more than 9,000 crores every single year.

But they still sell the same Namkeens as the 12-year-old boy in Bikaner.
